back: The services PE in Article 5(3)(b) (183 days in 12 months), wider source taxation of royalties and fees (Articles 12 and 12A in the UN Model 2021 numbering, now 12AA in the UN Model 2025), and Article 13(5) on gains on substantial shareholdings. Article 7 also keeps a limited force of attraction rule.

front: What does the 2025 UN Model update add, as at 2026?
back: Described in the Committee's work: a natural resources article (5A), a services article (12AA) replacing Articles 12A and 14, an insurance premiums article (12C) replacing Article 5(6), and a subject to tax provision in Article 1(3). Check the published text for article detail.

front: What process produced the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation?
back: General Assembly Resolutions 77/244 (2022) and 78/230 (2023) started it, terms of reference were adopted in 2024, and an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee negotiates the convention.

front: Which two early protocols are being negotiated alongside the UN Framework Convention?
back: One on the taxation of income from cross-border services in a digitalised and globalised economy, and one on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes.

front: What was the status of the UN Framework Convention as at 2026?
back: Under negotiation: drafts of the convention and two early protocols were released in July 2026 and discussed at the fifth INC session (ended 13 August 2026), with open disagreements, a sixth session in Nairobi from 30 November 2026 and final texts targeted for 2027. It is not yet in force.

front: What is the minimum rate and scope threshold of the GloBE rules?
back: A 15% minimum effective tax rate applying to groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million in at least two of the four preceding fiscal years.

front: What is the income inclusion rule (IIR) and how does it apply in a chain?
back: The main GloBE charging rule: a parent entity pays top-up tax on the low taxed income of its constituent entities. It applies top down, so the ultimate parent applies it first and, if it does not, the next intermediate parent does.

front: What is the UTPR and how is its top-up tax allocated?
back: The backstop charging rule, applying where low taxed income is not brought into charge by an IIR. The top-up tax is allocated among UTPR jurisdictions by a key based on employees and tangible assets, and collected by denying deductions or an equivalent adjustment.

front: What is a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT) and why does it matter?
back: A domestic top-up tax on the low taxed profits of entities located in a jurisdiction, creditable against IIR and UTPR top-up tax. It lets the source jurisdiction collect the tax first rather than another state.

front: In what order do the QDMTT, IIR and UTPR operate?
back: QDMTT first (source state collects), then the IIR top down, then the UTPR as the backstop. QDMTT paid reduces the top-up tax under the other two.

front: How is GloBE income computed?
back: Start with the financial accounting net income or loss in the consolidated accounts, then apply the Model Rules adjustments (for example excluded dividends and equity gains, policy disallowed expenses such as fines, and arm's length transfer pricing adjustments).

front: Which taxes are covered taxes for GloBE?
back: Taxes on income or profits, taxes imposed instead of them (such as certain withholding taxes), and taxes on retained earnings and corporate equity. VAT, payroll and property taxes are not covered.

front: How is the GloBE jurisdictional ETR calculated?
back: Total adjusted covered taxes of all constituent entities in the jurisdiction divided by their total net GloBE income. Entities in one jurisdiction are blended.

front: What is the top-up tax percentage and how does the substance based income exclusion affect the tax?
back: The top-up percentage is 15% minus the jurisdictional ETR. It applies to excess profit, which is net GloBE income less the SBIE (a percentage of eligible payroll and tangible assets).

front: What are the SBIE percentages in the first year of the GloBE rules?
back: 10% of eligible payroll costs and 8% of eligible tangible assets, declining over ten years to 5% of each.

front: Compute: net GloBE income 200, adjusted covered taxes 20, SBIE 12. What is the top-up tax?
back: ETR 20 ÷ 200 = 10%, top-up percentage 5%, excess profit 200 − 12 = 188, top-up tax 188 × 5% = 9.4.

front: What is the de minimis exclusion in the GloBE rules?
back: A jurisdiction is excluded if the group's average GloBE revenue there is below EUR 10 million and average GloBE income is below EUR 1 million.

front: How does the transitional CbCR safe harbour work?
back: For early years no top-up tax arises in a jurisdiction if qualified CbCR data meets a de minimis test, a simplified ETR test (15% for 2023 and 2024, 16% for 2025, 17% for 2026) or a routine profits test. The January 2026 package extends it by one year, to fiscal years beginning on or before 31 December 2027.

front: What was agreed on 5 January 2026 in the side-by-side package?
back: The Inclusive Framework agreed a package including a side-by-side system for groups with parents in jurisdictions with qualifying regimes (designed for the United States), a simplified ETR safe harbour, a substance based tax incentive safe harbour and a one-year transitional CbCR extension, with further anti-arbitrage work.

front: What is the criticism of the side-by-side system?
back: It departs from the common approach with uniform application, favouring groups parented in certain jurisdictions and adding complexity. Supporters say it keeps Pillar Two operating and preserves the consensus.

front: What is the subject to tax rule (STTR)?
back: A Pillar Two treaty rule letting a developing source state tax certain intragroup payments (interest, royalties and other defined payments) where the payee's nominal rate is below 9%, up to the difference between 9% and that rate.

front: How does the STTR differ from the GloBE rules in benchmark and legal form?
back: The STTR uses a 9% benchmark on a payment and is applied by the source state through treaties. GloBE uses 15% on a jurisdictional ETR and is applied through domestic law (IIR, UTPR, QDMTT).

front: Compute STTR tax: interest 1,000, payee's nominal rate 3%. What may the source state tax?
back: Top-up percentage 9% − 3% = 6%, so the source state may tax 6% × 1,000 = 60, within any treaty limit.

front: How does an STTR tax interact with GloBE?
back: It is treated as a covered tax of the payee, so it reduces any IIR or UTPR top-up tax for the payee's jurisdiction.

front: What is the STTR Multilateral Convention and its status as at 2026?
back: The Multilateral Convention to Facilitate the Implementation of the Pillar Two Subject to Tax Rule, opened for signature in 2024, lets parties apply the STTR to existing treaties without bilateral renegotiation. San Marino ratified first in 2025 and Albania's ratification as second (September 2026) brings it into force from 1 January 2027 according to the OECD; verify the parties on the depositary page.

front: What is Amount A and what is its scope?
back: A Pillar One right reallocating part of the profits of the largest groups to market jurisdictions without physical presence: groups with revenue above EUR 20 billion and profitability above 10%, excluding extractives and regulated financial services.

front: How much profit does Amount A reallocate and on what nexus?
back: 25% of profit above 10% of revenue, allocated to jurisdictions where the group has at least EUR 1 million of revenue (EUR 250,000 where GDP is below EUR 40 billion), using a revenue sourcing key.

front: Compute: revenue 100 billion, profit before tax 15 billion. What is the Amount A pool?
back: Residual profit 15 − 10 = 5 billion; 25% × 5 = 1.25 billion. A market with 4% of sourced revenue receives 0.05 billion.

front: What is Amount B?
back: A simplified and streamlined approach to the arm's length principle for baseline marketing and distribution activities, using a pricing matrix by industry grouping and asset and expense intensity. It is in an annex to Chapter IV of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines.

front: What was the status of Pillar One and the Amount A Multilateral Convention as at 2026?
back: The text was stabilised but the convention has not been finalised, members could not agree on mandatory Amount B, and the United States withdrew support in 2025. Pillar One is stalled, so the DST standstill is uncertain.

front: Why do states regulate transfer pricing?
back: Prices set between associated enterprises are not tested by the market and decide which state taxes the profit, so states reallocate profit to match economic activity under the arm's length principle (Article 9(1), OECD and UN Models).

front: State the arm's length principle.
back: Associated enterprises are taxed as if they were independent, by comparing their conditions with those independent enterprises would have agreed in comparable circumstances (Article 9(1)).

front: Give two arguments for and two against the arm's length principle.
back: For: it treats group and stand-alone businesses alike and has the widest treaty acceptance. Against: comparables often do not exist for unique intangibles, and it ignores group synergies while being costly to administer.

front: What is formulary apportionment?
back: Combined group profit is computed as one enterprise and divided between states by a formula, usually sales, assets and payroll. It is used between sub-national units such as US states but not as the basis of the OECD or UN Models.

front: What is the main weakness of formulary apportionment internationally?
back: It needs multilateral agreement on the base, factors and weights, otherwise double taxation or non-taxation arises, and the factors are arbitrary and can be planned around.

front: How is Pillar One Amount A related to formulary approaches?
back: Amount A is a formula-based reallocation of part of the residual profit of the very largest groups; it is a targeted addition and does not replace arm's length pricing for ordinary transactions. Its multilateral convention was never opened for signature.

front: What is the US statutory basis for transfer pricing and its intangibles standard?
back: Section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code allows the allocation of income between commonly controlled businesses; for intangibles it applies a 'commensurate with income' standard allowing later adjustment to actual income.

front: How does UK law relate to the OECD Guidelines?
back: Part 4 of TIOPA 2010 must be read consistently with the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, giving them legislative weight as an interpretive aid.

front: What distinctive feature does German practice have for cross-border moves of business functions?
back: The rules on transfer of functions (Funktionsverlagerung) price the whole package of functions, assets and profit potential moved, not just individual assets.

front: What distinctive power does Australian transfer pricing law give the Commissioner?
back: Division 815 allows reconstruction of an arrangement independent parties would not have entered into, and is expressed to be applied consistently with the OECD Guidelines.

front: What does Article 9(1) do and does it create a charge?
back: It allows profits that would have accrued but for non-arm's length conditions between associated enterprises to be included in an enterprise's profits. The charging power is domestic law; Article 9 confirms and limits it.

front: When are two enterprises associated under Article 9?
back: When one participates directly or indirectly in the management, control or capital of the other, or the same persons do so for both.

front: What does Article 9(2) require?
back: The other state must make an appropriate corresponding adjustment to the tax on profits already taxed there, but only if it agrees the primary adjustment is justified in principle and amount; competent authorities consult if needed.

front: What is the difference between a primary and a corresponding adjustment?
back: A primary adjustment increases profit in one state, creating economic double taxation; a corresponding adjustment in the other state reduces its profit or tax to relieve it (Article 9(2)).

front: What is UN Model Article 9(3)?
back: It denies the corresponding adjustment under Article 9(2) where a final ruling shows an enterprise is liable to penalty for fraud, gross negligence or wilful default. The OECD Model has no equivalent.

front: How is a corresponding adjustment pursued if the states disagree?
back: Through the mutual agreement procedure in Article 25. OECD Article 25(5): arbitration after two years if the person requests it in writing. UN Model: optional Article 25 Alternative B, arbitration after three years if either competent authority requests it.

front: Distinguish unilateral, bilateral and multilateral APAs.
back: Unilateral: taxpayer and one authority, certainty in one state only. Bilateral: two competent authorities under the MAP article, avoids double taxation. Multilateral: three or more authorities.

front: What are critical assumptions in an APA?
back: Facts on which the agreement rests; a material change allows revision or cancellation.

front: Which five methods are in OECD Guidelines Chapter II?
back: CUP, resale price and cost plus (traditional transaction methods), and TNMM and profit split (transactional profit methods).

front: What is the 'most appropriate method' rule?
back: Choose the method best suited to the facts given the functional analysis, data reliability and comparability; where a traditional method and a profit method are equally reliable, prefer the traditional method.

front: Describe the CUP method and when it is reliable.
back: It compares the controlled price with the price in a comparable uncontrolled transaction. It is most direct but needs close product and contract similarity; internal comparables are best.

front: Describe the resale price method.
back: Start with the resale price to an independent party and deduct an arm's length gross margin (and other costs) to reach the purchase price. It suits distributors adding little value.

front: Describe the cost plus method.
back: Take the supplier's costs in the controlled transaction and add an arm's length mark-up. It suits contract manufacturers and service providers.

front: What does TNMM compare, and who is the tested party?
back: The tested party's net profit indicator (for example operating margin) with that of comparable independent enterprises. The tested party should be the simplest one, with no unique intangibles.

front: When is the profit split method appropriate?
back: When each party makes unique and valuable contributions, operations are highly integrated, or the parties share assumption of economically significant risks (2018 guidance); split by contribution or residual analysis.

front: What are the five comparability factors?
back: Characteristics of property or services, functional analysis, contractual terms, economic circumstances, and business strategies (Chapter III).

front: How is the interquartile range used and where is the adjustment made?
back: It narrows a range with comparability defects to the 25th to 75th percentile; a result outside it is usually adjusted to the median, though some states adjust to the nearest edge.

front: TNMM test: sales 40,000,000, operating profit 1,200,000, comparable median margin 4.5% and interquartile range 3.3% to 5.65%. What is the adjustment?
back: Actual margin is 3.0%, below the range. Profit at the median is 1,800,000, so the adjustment is 600,000.

front: Cost plus: costs 12,500,000, median mark-up 8%. What is the price?
Who is entitled to intangible profit after BEPS Action 8?
back: Not automatically the legal owner: entitlement follows the DEMPE functions performed, assets used and risks controlled; other contributors are compensated at arm's length.

front: What does DEMPE stand for?
back: Development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation of an intangible (OECD Guidelines Chapter VI).

front: What are hard to value intangibles and what is the special rule?
back: Intangibles with no reliable comparables and highly uncertain projections at transfer. Tax administrations may use ex post results as presumptive evidence of the ex ante price, subject to exemptions in paragraph 6.193 such as a qualifying APA, a gap of no more than 20% of the compensation, or five years of commercialisation with a gap of no more than 20% of projections.

front: What return does a funder get if it does not control the financial risk?
back: Only a risk-free return on its funding, not the residual profit of the project (Chapter I, Chapter VI).

front: What is the benefit test for intra-group services?
back: Whether an independent enterprise in comparable circumstances would have paid for the service or performed it itself; shareholder activities and duplicative services give no chargeable benefit (Chapter VII).

front: How does the low value adding services simplified approach work?
back: Pool the relevant costs without shareholder items, allocate by a reasonable key, and add a 5% mark-up without benchmarking. Pool 700,000 gives a charge of 735,000.

front: What is a cost contribution arrangement?
back: A contractual arrangement to share the contributions and risks of developing assets, services or rights, where each participant's contribution is proportionate to its expected benefit, measured at value with balancing payments (Chapter VIII).

front: What risks do safe harbours carry according to the Guidelines?
back: Results may depart from arm's length, the other state may not accept them (double taxation), and they invite planning; they are suited to smaller taxpayers and simpler transactions (Chapter IV).

front: What are the six steps of the risk analysis framework (BEPS Action 9)?
back: Identify economically significant risks; contractual assumption; functional analysis of control and mitigation; interpret steps 1 to 3 (control plus financial capacity); allocate the risk; price the transaction.

front: What does Article 9(2), OECD and UN Models, require of the second state?
back: It must make an appropriate corresponding adjustment if it agrees the first state's adjustment is justified in principle and as to amount; the competent authorities consult if necessary. It is not automatic.

front: Within what period must a MAP case be presented under Article 25(1)?
back: Within three years of the first notification of the action giving rise to taxation not in accordance with the treaty, under the Model text (bilateral treaties vary, so check each one).

front: What is the duty of the competent authorities under Article 25(2)?
back: To endeavour to resolve the case by mutual agreement if the objection appears justified and they cannot solve it unilaterally. It is a duty of means, not of result.

front: When does OECD Article 25(5) allow arbitration?
back: If the competent authorities cannot resolve the case within two years from the date all required information has been provided to both, the unresolved issues go to arbitration at the request of the person who presented the case.

front: How does the UN Model treat arbitration in Article 25?
back: It offers two alternatives: Alternative A has no arbitration; Alternative B provides arbitration, if either competent authority so requests, where the competent authorities cannot agree within three years. States choose.

front: Which areas make up the BEPS Action 14 minimum standard on resolving treaty disputes (preventing disputes, MAP access, timely resolution and implementation)?
back: Prevent disputes, make MAP available and accessible, resolve cases in a timely manner (average target of 24 months, a target not a deadline, with MAP statistics published), and implement agreements reached. It does not require arbitration.

front: What is an advance pricing agreement (APA)?
back: An arrangement that fixes in advance the method, comparables, adjustments and critical assumptions for pricing controlled transactions over a set period (OECD Guidelines Chapter IV, Section F).

front: Why does the OECD favour bilateral over unilateral APAs?
back: A unilateral APA binds only one administration, so double taxation can remain; a bilateral APA is agreed by both competent authorities under the MAP article and removes it.

front: What happens if a critical assumption in an APA fails?
back: The APA may be revised or cancelled, since it depends on those assumptions holding during the period.

front: State the two steps of the authorised OECD approach (AOA) to PE profits.
back: Step one: a functional and factual analysis treats the PE as a separate enterprise and attributes assets, risks and capital by significant people functions. Step two: price the dealings by applying Article 9 and the Guidelines by analogy (OECD Article 7(2), 2010 Report).

front: What are 'significant people functions' in the AOA?
back: The functions that decide the assumption and management of risk and the use of assets; they determine where assets and risks are attributed to the PE.

front: How does the UN Model's Article 7 differ from the AOA?
back: It does not adopt the AOA in full: it keeps a limited force of attraction rule and restricts deductions for certain internal payments such as royalties, favouring the source state.

front: What did the 2018 Additional Guidance on attribution of profits to PEs address?
back: How Article 7 and the AOA apply to PEs created by the Action 7 changes to Article 5, including that a dependent agent PE's profit must not double count the agent enterprise's arm's length remuneration under Article 9.

front: Name the three tiers of BEPS Action 13 documentation.
back: The master file, the local file and the country by country report (Chapter V of the OECD Guidelines). Only the CbCR is a minimum standard.

front: What does the master file contain?
back: A high level overview of the group: organisational structure, description of the business, intangibles, intercompany financial activities, and financial and tax positions.

front: What does the local file contain?
back: Detailed information on the local entity's material controlled transactions: the transactions and amounts, functional and comparability analysis, the method chosen and financial information.

front: What is the CbCR filing threshold and who files?
back: Groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million in the preceding year; the ultimate parent files in its residence state, with exchange to other jurisdictions.

front: What are the three tables of the country by country report?
back: Table 1: revenue, profit, tax paid and accrued, capital, earnings, employees and tangible assets by jurisdiction. Table 2: constituent entities and their main activities. Table 3: additional information.

front: Can a tax administration make a transfer pricing adjustment based on the CbCR alone?
back: No. The CbCR is for high level risk assessment, not a substitute for transactional analysis and not a basis for formulary apportionment.

front: When is the CbCR due?
back: Within 12 months of the last day of the group's fiscal year, with a secondary local filing mechanism if the parent's state does not exchange or fails systematically.

front: What is the legal status of the UN Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries (2021)?
back: Non binding guidance by the UN Subcommittee on Transfer Pricing, not an official Commentary to the UN Model, setting out the UN's practical reading of the arm's length principle.

front: How does the UN Manual approach location savings compared with the OECD Guidelines?
back: Both treat them as comparability factors; the UN Manual stresses that the local entity should share in the savings, depending on what independent parties would agree, while the OECD uses local comparables or an allocation by functions, assets, risks and bargaining positions.

front: What is the 'sixth method'?
back: Used for quoted commodities between associated enterprises: the quoted price at shipment date is the arm's length price, with adjustments. It features in the UN Manual and some domestic laws, and is not one of the OECD's five methods.

front: What practical comparability problem do developing states face, and what does the UN Manual suggest?
back: Few reliable local comparables; it accepts adjusted comparables from other regions and warns against using undisclosed data the taxpayer cannot challenge.

front: What simplified approach does the OECD offer for low value adding intra group services?
back: A simplified approach with a 5% mark up on the cost pool (OECD Guidelines Chapter VII).

front: What does Article 24(4) say about deduction of interest paid to a non resident?
back: Interest is deductible under the same conditions as if paid to a resident, except where Article 9(1), Article 11(6) or Article 12(4) applies (Article 12(6) in the UN Model; same structure in both Models).

front: What does Article 11(6) do?
back: Where a special relationship makes the interest exceed what would have been agreed otherwise, Article 11 applies only to the arm's length amount; the excess remains taxable under domestic law with regard to other treaty provisions.

front: What did the CJEU decide in Lankhorst-Hohorst (2002)?
back: A German thin capitalisation rule applying only to non resident parent lenders infringed freedom of establishment.

front: What is the status of BEPS Action 4?
back: A best practice recommendation, not a minimum standard, so states may adopt it or a different rule.

front: State the Action 4 fixed ratio rule.
back: An entity's net interest deduction is limited to a fixed percentage of its tax EBITDA, within a recommended corridor of 10% to 30%, chosen by each state.

front: Why does Action 4 use net interest and tax EBITDA?
back: Net interest (interest expense minus interest income) measures actual financing cost, and tax EBITDA is earnings calculated under tax rules before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.

front: How does the Action 4 group ratio rule work?
back: An entity may deduct up to the group's net third party interest to EBITDA ratio times its own tax EBITDA, capped by the group's total net third party interest; it is optional and lets genuinely leveraged groups deduct more.

front: List the optional Action 4 elements.
back: A de minimis threshold (EUR 2 million is often quoted as an example; each state sets its own), carry forward of disallowed interest and unused capacity, targeted anti avoidance rules, and exclusions such as public benefit infrastructure.

front: Calculate: tax EBITDA 10,000,000, net interest 4,500,000, fixed ratio 30%. What is disallowed?
back: Cap = 30% × 10,000,000 = 3,000,000, so 1,500,000 is disallowed (subject to carry forward and the de minimis threshold).

front: Group net third party interest 90,000,000, group EBITDA 200,000,000, entity tax EBITDA 10,000,000. What is the group ratio cap?
back: Group ratio = 45%, so the cap = 45% × 10,000,000 = 4,500,000, higher than a 30% fixed ratio cap of 3,000,000.

front: How are banks and insurers treated under the Action 4 work?
back: The general rule suits them poorly because interest is their ordinary business, so they are treated separately, through regulatory capital rules, adapted rules or specific rules chosen by each state.

front: Why must a thin capitalisation rule be applied to domestic and foreign debt alike?
back: To avoid breaching Article 24(4) non-discrimination (and, in the EU, freedom of establishment); the Action 4 report recommends this design.

front: Does a denied interest deduction change the Article 11 withholding tax limit?
back: No. The Article 11(2) cap (10% in the OECD Model; rate left to negotiation in the UN Model) still applies to interest actually paid unless domestic law recharacterises it as a dividend.

front: What are the two targets of the OECD's 1998 harmful tax competition report?
back: Tax havens and harmful preferential tax regimes. It created the Forum on Harmful Tax Practices (FHTP) to review regimes.

front: What are the four key factors used to identify a harmful preferential regime?
back: No or low effective tax rate (the gateway factor), ring-fencing, lack of transparency, and lack of effective exchange of information.

front: What is ring-fencing in the FHTP framework?
back: A regime is ring-fenced if it is partly or fully insulated from the domestic market, either by excluding residents from the benefit or by barring beneficiaries from operating domestically.

front: Name four of the 'other factors' the FHTP uses as supporting evidence of harm.
back: For example: artificial definition of the tax base, failure to follow transfer pricing principles, a negotiable rate or base, secrecy provisions, a wide treaty network, promotion as a tax minimisation vehicle, purely tax driven operations with no substantial activity.

front: Which four BEPS Actions are minimum standards?
back: Action 5 (harmful tax practices), Action 6 (treaty abuse), Action 13 (transfer pricing documentation and CbC reporting) and Action 14 (dispute resolution).

front: What are the two main components of the Action 5 minimum standard?
back: The substantial activity requirement (applied to IP regimes through the nexus approach) and the transparency framework of compulsory spontaneous exchange of rulings.

front: What is the nexus approach for IP regimes?
back: Benefits are allowed only to the extent the taxpayer itself incurred qualifying R&D expenditure that gave rise to the IP income, using that expenditure as the proxy for substantial activity.

front: State the nexus ratio.
back: (Qualifying expenditures + uplift) ÷ overall expenditures on the IP asset; multiplied by overall IP income it gives the income that may benefit from the regime.

front: How is the nexus uplift calculated?
back: The lesser of 30% of qualifying expenditures and the non-qualifying expenditures (overall minus qualifying).

front: Which IP assets qualify under the nexus approach?
back: Patents and functionally equivalent IP assets (non-obvious, useful, novel, legally protected); copyrighted software for small taxpayers. Marketing IP such as trademarks does not qualify.

front: Nexus example: qualifying expenditure 700, non-qualifying 300, IP income 500. What income benefits?
back: Uplift = lesser of 210 and 300 = 210. Ratio = 910 ÷ 1,000 = 91%. Benefiting income = 91% × 500 = 455.

front: What categories of ruling does the Action 5 transparency framework cover?
back: Rulings on preferential regimes; unilateral cross-border APAs and transfer pricing rulings; downward profit adjustments not reflected in the accounts; PE rulings; related party conduit rulings; plus any other ruling type the FHTP later agrees.

front: What happened to grandfathering of existing IP regimes under Action 5?
back: Existing IP regimes were closed to new entrants from 30 June 2016 and grandfathered benefits ended on 30 June 2021.

front: Why is Action 5 described as peer reviewed rather than enforced?
back: The FHTP monitors implementation and publishes results; the pressure is reputational and political, plus defensive measures other states may take, not a formal sanction.

front: What does a CFC rule do?
back: It attributes certain income of a low-taxed foreign company controlled by residents to those resident shareholders, taxing them currently whether or not it is distributed.

front: What is the difference between the transactional and jurisdictional approach to CFC rules?
back: Transactional rules attribute defined categories of income (such as passive income); jurisdictional rules apply where the CFC is in a listed or low tax state. Many states combine them.

front: How do foreign personal holding company rules differ from CFC rules?
back: FPHC rules turn on closely held ownership and mainly passive income; CFC rules turn on control and the income type or foreign tax level. PFIC rules also reach minority holders.

front: List the six building blocks of effective CFC rules in Action 3.
back: Definition of a CFC; exemptions and thresholds; definition of CFC income; rules for computing income; rules to attribute income; rules to prevent and eliminate double taxation.

front: Is Action 3 a minimum standard?
back: No. Action 3 sets out recommendations (building blocks) for CFC rule design; states remain free to design their own rules.

front: What control tests may a CFC definition use under Action 3?
back: Legal control, economic control, de facto control, or a combination; related party holdings may be aggregated, and control above 50% is the typical level.

front: Name three approaches to defining CFC income discussed in Action 3.
back: Categorical analysis, substance analysis and excess profits analysis.

front: CFC example: CFC income 300, parent holds 60%, parent rate 25%, foreign tax on CFC income 5%. What is the net home tax?
back: Attributed 60% × 300 = 180; tax 45; credit 5% × 300 × 60% = 9; net tax 36.

front: Why are CFC rules generally held not to conflict with Article 7 of the OECD Model?
back: Article 7 limits taxation of the foreign company's profits by the source state; a CFC rule taxes the resident shareholder on attributed income, so it is not a tax on the foreign enterprise (OECD Commentary on Article 1).

front: What did the CJEU decide in Cadbury Schweppes (2006)?
back: CFC rules restricting freedom of establishment can be justified only if they target wholly artificial arrangements, so EU states added a substance or motive exception.

front: What are the three outcomes of a hybrid mismatch in Action 2?
back: Deduction/no inclusion (D/NI), double deduction (DD) and indirect D/NI (imported mismatch).

front: Give four of the five types of hybrid mismatch arrangement.
back: Hybrid financial instruments, hybrid transfers (such as repos), disregarded payments by hybrid entities, payments to reverse hybrids, and dual resident entities.

front: State the primary and defensive rule for a D/NI mismatch.
back: Primary: the payer state denies the deduction to the extent the payment is not included in ordinary income in the payee state. Defensive: if not denied, the payee state includes it in ordinary income.

front: State the primary and defensive rule for a double deduction.
back: Primary: the parent (investor) state denies the deduction; defensive: the payer state denies it. Dual inclusion income can absorb the deduction.

front: What is dual inclusion income?
back: Income that is included in ordinary income in both states, against which a double deduction may be allowed.

front: When do the Action 2 hybrid rules apply to payments?
back: Between related parties in a control group (a 25% test, extended to 50% for some rules) and under structured arrangements priced to reflect the mismatch.

front: What timing difference is tolerated under the Action 2 rules?
back: No mismatch arises if the payment is included in ordinary income within a reasonable period, which the report suggests is 12 months from the end of the payer's accounting period.

front: Which OECD Model changes did Action 2 recommend?
back: Commentary on Article 1 for transparent entities, Article 4(3) so competent authorities decide the residence of dual resident entities by mutual agreement (the UN Model 2025 also uses this approach), and Article 23 so exemption does not apply to income deductible in the source state.

front: Hybrid example: State S deducts 100 interest at 25%; State R treats the payment as an exempt dividend. What does the primary rule do?
back: State S denies the 100 deduction, adding 100 × 25% = 25 to Sub Co's tax and neutralising the mismatch.

front: What is an imported mismatch?
back: A payment deductible in one state funds a deductible hybrid payment elsewhere; the rule denies the deduction so the mismatch effect is not imported into the payer's state.

front: What are the three pillars of the BEPS Project?
back: Coherence of domestic rules (Actions 2 to 5), alignment of taxation with substance (Actions 5 to 10) and transparency, certainty and predictability (Actions 11 to 14), with Actions 1 and 15 cross cutting.

front: What do Actions 8 to 10 cover?
back: Aligning transfer pricing outcomes with value creation: intangibles (8), risks and capital (9) and other high risk transactions (10).

front: What is Action 4 and what status do its outputs have?
back: Limiting base erosion through interest deductions; the best practice recommendation is a fixed ratio rule of 10% to 30% of tax EBITDA, optionally with a group ratio rule.

front: What is the purpose of Action 11 and its status?
back: To measure and monitor BEPS through indicators and data analysis; it is a monitoring mandate, not a rule or minimum standard.

front: Which body is the main international standard setter on money laundering, and what did its 2012 revision add on tax?
back: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF). Its 2012 revised Recommendations listed serious tax crimes among the designated predicate offences for money laundering.

front: What is a predicate offence in money laundering law?
back: The underlying crime that generates the criminal property, here serious tax evasion. Without a predicate offence there is nothing to launder.

front: Why is the distinction between evasion and avoidance central to the tax and money laundering link?
back: Only evasion (dishonest non-disclosure or a false statement) is a crime and so can be a predicate offence. Avoidance, however aggressive, is not.

front: What is the revenue rule, and which English case is the usual authority?
back: Courts of one state do not enforce the tax claims of another. The usual authority is Government of India v Taylor (House of Lords, 1955).

front: What did Pasquantino v United States (2005) decide?
back: The US Supreme Court held that a scheme to defraud a foreign government of tax revenue, using US wires, could be prosecuted as wire fraud, and the revenue rule did not prevent it.

front: What is dual criminality in the context of foreign fiscal offences?
back: The conduct must be an offence both where it occurred and in the state asked to act, so a state that criminalises equivalent evasion of its own taxes can usually treat foreign evasion as qualifying.

front: What information standard does Article 26 of the OECD Model set?
back: Information that is foreseeably relevant for applying the convention or administering and enforcing domestic tax laws. The phrase replaced 'necessary' in the 2005 update.

front: Has the UN Model adopted the same relevance standard as the OECD Model in Article 26?
back: Yes. The UN Model's 2011 update aligned Article 26 with the foreseeably relevant wording, so the two Models are now very close on the standard.

front: Is Article 26 exchange limited to residents or to taxes covered by the treaty?
back: No. It is not limited by Article 1 (persons covered) or Article 2 (taxes covered); it extends to taxes of every kind imposed by or on behalf of the contracting states.

front: Can a requested state refuse an Article 26 request because the information is held by a bank?
back: No. Paragraph 5 of OECD Article 26 (added in 2005, with a UN equivalent) bars refusal solely because information is held by a bank, nominee, agent or fiduciary or concerns ownership interests.

front: Does a requested state need a domestic tax interest in the information before it must act under Article 26?
back: No. The requested state must use its information gathering powers to answer the request even where it has no domestic tax interest.

front: List the three modes of exchange of information.
back: On request (specific and targeted), spontaneous (volunteered because it may be relevant to the other state) and automatic (systematic bulk transmission of predefined information at regular intervals).

front: What is a fishing expedition and why is it not permitted under Article 26?
back: A speculative request with no link to an identified taxpayer, group or investigation. Foreseeable relevance requires such a link, although group requests that identify a pattern of behaviour can be valid.

front: To whom may information received under Article 26 be disclosed?
back: Persons or authorities, including courts, concerned with assessment, collection, enforcement, prosecution, appeals or oversight of the taxes. The OECD text allows other uses if both states' laws permit and the supplying authority authorises.

front: Name three grounds on which a state may decline to supply information under Article 26.
back: Administrative measures contrary to its law or practice, information not obtainable under either state's laws, and trade, business or professional secrets or information contrary to public policy (ordre public).

front: What is a TIEA and what does the OECD Model TIEA (2002) provide?
back: A tax information exchange agreement dealing only with information. The Model provides exchange on request, with no domestic interest requirement, covering civil and criminal matters, and bank and ownership information, with safeguards against fishing expeditions.

front: Does a TIEA give relief from double taxation?
back: No. It creates no taxing rights and gives no relief; it is a purely administrative instrument.

front: What is the Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes and how does it work?
back: A wide membership body, restructured in 2009, that peer reviews jurisdictions' legal frameworks (Phase 1) and practice (Phase 2) against the exchange standards and issues ratings.

front: What are the Global Forum's overall peer review ratings?
back: Compliant, Largely Compliant, Partially Compliant and Non-Compliant.

front: Which standards does the Global Forum monitor?
back: The two international standards: exchange of information on request and automatic exchange of financial account information under the Common Reporting Standard. Beneficial ownership transparency is assessed as part of the on request standard.

front: What are the three tiers of BEPS Action 13 documentation?
back: The master file (group overview), the local file (local entity's related party transactions) and the country-by-country report (revenue, profit, tax and activity data per jurisdiction).

front: What is the CbC reporting threshold and how is it tested?
back: Consolidated group revenue of EUR 750 million (or local currency equivalent) in the preceding fiscal year. The test looks back one year.

front: Where is a CbC report normally filed and how does it reach other tax authorities?
back: By the ultimate parent in its jurisdiction of residence, then exchanged automatically under qualifying competent authority agreements. Secondary or local filing applies if the parent's state does not require or exchange it.

front: How may tax authorities use CbC data?
back: For high level transfer pricing and BEPS risk assessment, not as conclusive evidence of transfer pricing outcomes, and not as a basis for formulary apportionment of income.

front: Is the United States a participant in the Common Reporting Standard?
back: No. The US operates FATCA through intergovernmental agreements (Model 1 and Model 2) and does not exchange under the CRS.

front: What triggers CRS reporting on an individual account holder: citizenship or residence?
back: Tax residence. A reportable person is resident in a reportable jurisdiction; citizenship is not the trigger.

front: How are passive non-financial entities treated under the CRS?
back: The financial institution looks through to the controlling persons, defined by reference to the FATF beneficial owner concept, and reports those resident in a reportable jurisdiction.

front: What due diligence applies to pre-existing individual accounts under the CRS?
back: Lower value accounts (up to USD 1,000,000) can be reviewed by electronic record search for indicia; high value accounts (above USD 1,000,000) need an enhanced review including a paper search and inquiry of the relationship manager.

front: What are the main 2023 amendments to the CRS?
back: Approved June 2023: coverage of electronic money products and central bank digital currencies, indirect crypto-asset investment, stronger due diligence and reporting outcomes, and an optional exclusion for genuine non-profits. Start dates vary by jurisdiction.

front: What does the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) cover?
back: Reporting crypto-asset service providers must report transactions in relevant crypto-assets, such as exchanges with fiat currency or other crypto-assets, using CRS style due diligence and automatic exchange. First-wave jurisdictions, including the EU through DAC8, apply it from 1 January 2026, with first exchanges in 2027; later waves follow from 2028.

front: What does Article 27 of the OECD and UN Models provide?
back: Assistance in the collection of taxes: the requested state collects the other state's enforceable revenue claim as its own debt, and may take conservancy measures. Exceptions apply for public policy and disproportionate burden.

front: Why is Article 27 needed as a treaty provision?
back: Because of the revenue rule, a foreign tax debt is not otherwise collectable abroad. The treaty creates the exception.

front: What forms of assistance does the Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters provide?
back: Exchange on request, spontaneous and automatic; simultaneous tax examinations and examinations abroad; assistance in recovery and conservancy; and service of documents.

front: Who developed the Multilateral Convention and what did the 2010 Protocol change?
back: The OECD and the Council of Europe, opened for signature in 1988. The 2010 Protocol (in force 2011) aligned it with the Article 26 standard and opened it to all states.

front: What does BEPS Action 12 recommend, and is it a minimum standard?
back: A modular framework for mandatory disclosure of aggressive or abusive arrangements, designed by choosing who reports, which hallmarks apply, timing and penalties. It is best practice, not a minimum standard.

front: Which MLI provisions are minimum standards, and which provision do most states use to meet the treaty abuse standard?
back: The preamble (Article 6), treaty abuse (Article 7) and dispute resolution (Article 16). Most states meet Article 7 through the principal purposes test alone.

front: When does the MLI actually modify a bilateral treaty?
back: Only where the treaty is a covered tax agreement notified by both parties and their choices and reservations match on the provision. Practitioners use matching tables or synthesised texts.

front: How does beneficial ownership for AML and transparency differ from beneficial owner in Articles 10, 11 and 12?
back: For AML it means the natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity. In Articles 10 to 12 it concerns entitlement to treaty benefits and has a distinct, treaty specific meaning.

front: What is the destination basis for VAT?
back: Tax is levied where goods or services are consumed: exports are zero-rated and imports taxed on entry, so imported and domestic goods bear the same tax in the market of consumption.

front: What is the origin basis for VAT and why is it less favoured?
back: Tax is levied where goods are produced, so exports carry the exporter's tax and imports enter free. It distorts competition where rates differ, so the destination basis is the international norm.

front: Why can an income tax treaty not be applied to VAT?
back: OECD and UN Model Article 2 limits the Models to taxes on income and on capital, so VAT falls outside them.

front: What is border tax adjustment and which taxes may be adjusted?
back: It is relief of tax on exports and a matching charge on imports. The 1970 GATT working party view is that indirect taxes such as VAT may be adjusted but direct taxes such as income tax may not.

front: What does GATT Article III require of internal taxes?
back: National treatment: imports must not be taxed in excess of like domestic products, and taxes must not be applied so as to protect domestic production.

front: How does the SCM Agreement treat export tax relief?
back: Subsidies contingent on export performance are prohibited. Under Annex I, remission of indirect taxes beyond those borne by the domestic product, and certain exemptions of direct tax on export income, count as export subsidies.

front: What did the WTO decide in the US foreign sales corporation dispute?
back: The Appellate Body held that the regime, which exempted part of export income from direct tax, was a prohibited export subsidy.

front: What is GATS Article XIV(d)?
back: A general exception for measures aimed at the equitable or effective imposition or collection of direct taxes, including residence-based differences, provided they are not arbitrary or a disguised restriction.

front: Outline WTO dispute settlement under the DSU.
back: Consultations, a panel, appeal on law to the Appellate Body, adoption of reports and, if a member does not comply, authorised retaliation. The Appellate Body has been unable to hear new appeals since late 2019.

front: List the main tax problems of a cross-border merger.
back: A dry charge on gains from a share or asset transfer, exit tax on assets leaving the jurisdiction, loss of tax attributes, shareholder-level gains on the exchange, and treaty source taxation of share gains.

front: What is exit taxation?
back: A charge by a state on unrealised gains when assets or residence leave its taxing jurisdiction, because it will have no later right to tax those gains.

front: What did the CJEU decide in National Grid Indus on exit tax?
back: Fixing the gain at exit is permitted, but immediate collection of tax on unrealised gains can breach freedom of establishment, so the taxpayer should be offered deferral or instalments.

front: What does the EU Merger Directive provide and what limits it?
back: Deferral of tax for qualifying mergers, divisions, asset transfers and share exchanges within the EU. It requires carry-over of tax values, a continuing PE link for assets and has an anti-avoidance clause.

front: How can a treaty relieve a cross-border share exchange?
back: Bilateral treaties can include clauses, as the Article 13 Commentary contemplates, so a reorganisation gain is not taxed where domestic law gives deferral. Few treaties contain them.

front: Which Articles may tax a gain on shares in a merger?
back: Article 13(4) of both Models for property-rich shares and, in the UN Model only, Article 13(5) for substantial holdings in a resident company. The UN Model 2025 has eight paragraphs in Article 13, the OECD Model five.

front: What is the status of the OECD COVID-19 treaty analysis?
back: It is Secretariat analysis (April 2020, updated January 2021), not an amendment of the Commentary, so it is persuasive guidance on applying existing Articles in exceptional circumstances.

front: How did the OECD COVID analysis treat employees stranded abroad under Article 15?
back: Days of unforeseen presence caused by government measures could be treated as days in the usual place of work for the 183 day test in Article 15(2), and bilateral agreements often applied this to border workers.

front: Did a COVID-forced home office create a PE under Article 5?
back: The Secretariat view was no: the temporary use of a home under government health measures was not a fixed place of business at the enterprise's disposal, and a stranded agent's activity was not habitual authority.

front: How did the OECD COVID analysis treat company residence under Article 4(3)?
back: A temporary change in where directors sat, caused by the crisis, should not change the Article 4(3) outcome (competent authority agreement in both Models, with place of effective management only one factor), and stranded individuals could keep their previous residence under the permanent home tests.

front: Name three tax issues raised by crypto-assets and by AI.
back: Characterisation as property, trading stock or payment instrument, no physical location for residence and source, and enforcement (the OECD CARF). For AI: PE attribution, since Article 5(5) needs a person, and transfer pricing of algorithms as intangibles.

front: What is the length and structure of the ADIT Principles of International Taxation (Module 1) paper?
back: The paper lasts 3 hours 15 minutes with no separate reading time. Part A has three essay-type questions and Part B two scenario-type questions, each worth 25 marks (Part A had five questions before the 2025 exams).

front: How many questions must you answer, and from which parts?
back: Four in total, with at least two from Part A and at least one from Part B.

front: How are marks spread across questions?
back: Every question is marked out of 25, so each is worth a quarter of the paper and deserves about a quarter of the time.

front: What time plan fits 195 minutes?
back: About 45 minutes per question including planning (4 × 45 = 180), leaving 15 minutes for choosing questions at the start and checking at the end (195 minus 180).

front: Is the ADIT paper open book?
back: No, it is closed book apart from the permitted books (such as the OECD Model including the 2025 Update, the UN Model (2021 edition listed for 2026, later editions allowed, so state which numbering you use), the TP Guidelines 2022, the MLI and its Explanatory Statement, the Pillar documents listed by the CIOT, the VCLT, Van Raad) and the PDFs on the exam platform.

front: Do you need detailed case citations?
back: No, you may cite cases and sources by their general name without detailed citations, but you must state the point they make and give the correct Article or source.

front: Does reciting an Article or Commentary passage earn marks?
back: No, marks are not given for reciting verbatim. They reward critical analysis and problem solving, marked holistically.

front: What are the six parts of a good essay answer?
back: Issue, rule and source, OECD versus UN, arguments both ways, application, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question.

front: Why must an essay answer discuss the UN Model as well as the OECD Model?
back: Both Models have equal prominence in the syllabus, and they differ on points such as permanent establishment and royalties, so a comparative point earns marks that an OECD-only answer misses.

front: What makes a conclusion weak in an essay answer?
back: Merely saying there are arguments on both sides. A strong conclusion says which side is stronger and why.

front: Give the steps for answering a treaty scenario.
back: Identify the taxpayer and income, determine residence, check treaty availability, pick the distributive article, state the limitation, apply relief (Article 23A or 23B), consider anti-abuse, then procedure.

front: How is dual residence of an individual resolved in a scenario?
back: Apply the treaty tie-breaker in Article 4(2) of the Model: permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, then mutual agreement.

front: Why raise anti-abuse in every treaty scenario?
back: Treaty benefit may be denied or limited by a principal purpose test, a limitation on benefits clause, a beneficial ownership requirement or domestic anti-avoidance rules, and omitting it is a common lost mark.

front: In a scenario, how should numbers be presented?
back: Show the working in clear lines, state assumptions, and use illustrative rates only if the question gives them or you flag them as assumed.

front: What is the effect of Article 23B on relief in a scenario?
back: The residence State gives a credit limited to the lower of the source State tax paid and its own tax on that income, so with 80 paid and 100 due it collects 20.

front: How does exemption under Article 23A differ numerically from credit?
back: With exemption the residence State exempts the income, so total tax is only the source State tax (80 in the worked example), whereas credit gives total tax at the higher rate (100).

front: How should you use the permitted texts during the exam?
back: Find the Article by name first, confirm its number, and compare the OECD and UN provision. Prepare beforehand by learning the layout so retrieval takes seconds.

front: Why practise with the exact versions of the permitted texts?
back: Article numbers, Commentary paragraph numbers and layout change between editions, so using the wrong version wastes time and risks misquotation.

front: Name three common mistakes in ADIT answers.
back: Listing without analysis, ignoring the UN Model, and ignoring anti-abuse rules. Others are answering the topic instead of the question and omitting the conclusion.

front: What should you do if you reach 45 minutes and are unfinished?
back: Write a short conclusion and move on, returning later if time allows. A brief conclusion is worth more than extra unfinished analysis.

front: What are the syllabus weights as this book states them?
back: Section I 20%, Sections II and III together 30%, Section IV 20%, Section V 25%, Section VI 5%, totalling 100% (check the current ADIT syllabus for the exact weights).

front: How should revision time follow the weights?
back: Roughly in proportion, adjusted for weakness, with extra application practice on the Level 3 content that makes up most of Sections II to V, and no section skipped entirely.

front: How should the Commentaries be treated when writing an answer?
back: As an interpretive aid, not binding law. Their weight differs between States, so say so when the point matters, and remember the VCLT general rule of interpretation.

front: What is the pass mark for the paper?
back: This chapter's sources do not state one, so check the CIOT's current guidance before sitting and do not rely on unofficial figures.
